title: SILAGE MAKING
text:
SILAGE MAKING

o Method of conserving animal feed for those times when there is less animal feed available.
o Corn, Napier, and other forage crops fermented.
o Sugars present in the fodder are converted to lactic acid, which acts as a preservative and a good source of readily fermentable sugars for the rumen microbes.

Advantage of silage making:
1. Keeps forage in good condition for a very long time without an excessive loss of feed nutrients.
2. Provides high-quality ruminant feed during extensive weather conditions.

Silage preparation:
1. Silage bag
2. Silage Bunker

Steps in silage making:
1. Harvesting
o Corn, Napier and other forage crops can be used for silage making.
2. Chopping
o Standard cut size 3/4 to 1 inch.
o Make sure that the harvested crop is about 65%-75% moisture content.
o Hand method used to estimate the moisture concentration of forage to be ensiled. Take a handful of chopped forage; squeeze it into a ball, and release.
o Chopped forage is too wet to ensile if the ball stays together and too dry if it quickly falls apart. Forage that slowly falls apart is ready to be ensiled.

Perform hand method to check the moisture of the forage.

3. Filling the silage bag

facts: Silage making is a method of conserving animal feed for times when less animal feed is available.
Corn, Napier, and other forage crops are fermented to make silage.
Sugars present in the fodder are converted into lactic acid during fermentation.
Lactic acid acts as a preservative and provides a good source of readily fermentable sugars for rumen microbes.
Silage making keeps forage in good condition for a very long time without excessive loss of feed nutrients.
Silage provides high-quality ruminant feed during extensive weather conditions.
Two forms or structures for silage preparation mentioned are silage bag and silage bunker.
The first step in silage making is harvesting.
The second step in silage making is chopping.
The standard cut size for chopping forage for silage is 3/4 to 1 inch.
Harvested crop for silage should have a moisture content of about 65% to 75%.
The hand method can be used to estimate the moisture concentration of forage to be ensiled.
To perform the hand moisture test, take a handful of chopped forage, squeeze it into a ball, and release.
In the hand squeeze test, forage is too wet to ensile if the ball stays together.
In the hand squeeze test, forage is too dry if the ball quickly falls apart.
In the hand squeeze test, forage is ready to be ensiled if the ball slowly falls apart.
The third step in silage making is filling the silage bag.
